S1Q04F.q: How would you reduce the sorting cost for millions of customers while preserving the tie rule?
S1Q04F.spoken: I would replace the full sort with a linear-time partial sort using argpartition to drop the complexity from O(N log N) to O(N) for millions of customers. To preserve the original row-order tie rule efficiently, I'd use a composite key pairing each score with its inverted row index, which makes the partial sort deterministic without requiring a heavy stable sort.

S1Q08.q: Now add delayed outcomes and experimentation, extend that design so churn outcomes arrive thirty days later, and retention offers affect the labels you observe. Design the prediction logging, the experiment assignment, the outcome joins, and how you select data for retraining.
S1Q08.spoken: For prediction logging, I record every scored user ID alongside the feature snapshot hash, model version, and timestamp to our warehouse. For experiment assignment, I use deterministic hashing on the subscriber ID and campaign salt right before scoring to split users into treatment and control groups. For outcome joins, I wait thirty days and join the lagging subscription status back to the prediction log using the execution date and subscriber ID. Finally, for retraining data selection, I exclude or inverse-propensity weight users who received retention offers so the model accounts for the intervention and avoids label bias.

S2Q05F.q: An example where that greedy policy gives poor coverage, and tell me how you would incorporate redundancy or multi hop dependencies.
S2Q05F.spoken: Imagine a financial audit where a question requires both the Q3 revenue figure and a risk disclaimer located in a separate appendix. If two chunks from the revenue section score slightly higher than the appendix chunk, a pure greedy selector fills the budget with redundant revenue text and drops the risk data entirely. To incorporate redundancy, I apply Maximal Marginal Relevance to penalize semantic duplicates and enforce source spread. For multi-hop dependencies, I use agentic query decomposition to break complex questions into sequential sub-queries, retrieving evidence iteratively across hops so each step fills the gaps of the last.

S2Q08.q: Migrate the embedding model without an outage, extend that service to introduce embeddings with a different dimensionality, while documents keep changing throughout the migration. Describe the versioning, the backfill, how updates stay synchronized, the quality comparison, the cutover, and the rollback.
S2Q08.spoken: I namespace collections by model version in our vector store, maintaining dual write pipelines that tag every chunk with its specific model ID. A background Airflow job processes historical documents in batches, generating new embeddings and populating the new collection asynchronously. Live document updates stream through our change data capture pipeline to trigger parallel workers that update both indexes simultaneously. We run shadow evaluations using offline test sets and retrieval metrics to verify that the new vector space matches or exceeds baseline accuracy. The cutover happens via a feature flag in our retrieval gateway once backfill parity and shadow tests pass. Finally, rollback is instantaneous by simply pointing the gateway back to the legacy collection if any latency or error anomalies occur.

Finally, since Azure OpenAI processes data locally within the provisioned region with no data sharing for training, we maintain full compliance without sacrificing inference performance.

C4.q: Going back to what you said about the tie rule, would that still hold with float scores from two models?
C4.spoken: Yes, it actually becomes even more critical with float scores from two models. Because outputs from different architectures have distinct scales and precision limits, score collisions happen frequently at decision boundaries. Without a deterministic secondary sorting key—like an ID or a base confidence score—ranking instability will silently corrupt your top-k evaluation.

C5.q: Going back to reciprocal rank fusion, how would you tune the constant c?
C5.spoken: I tune the constant c empirically using an offline evaluation set optimized for NDCG or MRR. A smaller c heavily prioritizes the top ranks, while a higher default like 60 smooths the distribution so lower-ranked matches still matter. I typically grid-search values between 10 and 100 against our gold queries to find the sweet spot.

D2.q: An example where that greedy policy gives poor coverage, and tell me how you would incorporate redundancy or multi hop dependencies.
D2.spoken: Imagine a financial audit query about a parent company's liabilities and a subsidiary's indemnity clause; a greedy retriever often pulls the top five chunks all from the parent section because of high semantic overlap, completely missing the subsidiary details. To fix this, I incorporate redundancy by applying Maximal Marginal Relevance to penalize repetitive chunks and enforce thematic diversity. For multi-hop dependencies, I use agentic query decomposition where the system resolves the first sub-question and uses its output to dynamically parameterize the search for the next hop.
